newsitem.title: UK: Cattles confident after 20 pct profit rise.
newsitem.headline: Cattles confident after 20 pct profit rise.

text.p: British financial services group Cattles Plc on Tuesday reported a 20 percent rise in profits for 1996 and said it was confident it could match this in 1997.
"I have to say we are reasonably happy with that (growth in profits)," Cattles' chief executive Eddie Cran told Reuters, adding he thought the group could maintain this in the year ahead.

Cattles' pretax profits rose to 33.9 million pounds ($54.8 million) from 28.2 million in 1995. It raised its total dividend to 8.3 pence from 6.9 pence and earnings per share to 17.0 pence from 14.0 pence.
Although the market initially reacted well to the figures, with a five pence rise in the group's share price, Cattles shares were marked down a penny at 315.5 pence at 1500 GMT.

The group, whose main business remains door-to-door moneylending to people who cannot normally borrow from mainstream lenders, said that by the end of the decade 50 percent of its profits will be generated from other areas of business.
In 1996, 65 percent of Cattles' profits came from its Shopacheck weekly home collected credit business. Prior to 1994, it had been 90 percent, the group said.

Cran said Shopacheck had had "a pretty good year" but that although the addition of 16,000 new customers was in line with his expectations, the door-to-door business was "not a massive growth business".

He said the big expansion for Cattles during 1996 had come from Welcome, which it bought in 1994. Welcome has a branch network and lends to people who are more likely to have a bank account and be employed but for a variety of reasons cannot or do not want to borrow from mainstream lenders such as banks.
Cran said Welcome had increased its receivables book by 28 percent to 108 million pounds in 1996 and had opened 11 new branches. Welcome's customer base increased to 45,000 from 37,000.

He said the return had more than doubled since 1994 and Cattles would therefore be paying the maximum deferred consideration of 3.5 million pounds to previous owners life and corporate pensions company London & Manchester in November 1997.
"The business has got incredible prospects," Cran said, adding that Welcome was an ideal means for lending the cash generated by Shopacheck.
Shopaplan, which offers people goods on credit rather than money, had not grown over the year but had incurred costs because it had been split from Shopacheck.
Cran said Shopaplan "has got to increase its return over the next year or two" and that recent personnel changes would help in this. He said it could be a useful "front-end" part of the group.
Cattles' corporate business, which includes factoring -- or buying a company's invoices at a discount before they are paid -- would also have to "grow quite significantly".
"I expect it (Reedham Factors) to double its profit over the next two to three years," Cran said. This development had involved taking on extra staff and space.
Cattles' finance and leasing division had a static year, both in terms of growth and profitability but the group said it expected to see a resumption of increased profitability in 1997.

Cran said the division had lost 120,000 pounds through one bad debt, and had been only one of many companies hit by the same fraud in the trailer rental sector. But this area was normally very profitable and Cattles would continue to finance it.
He said Cattles had grown organically over the year but did not rule out acquisitions if they offered a short-cut and were earnings enhancing.
